newsitem.title: USA: U.S. banking bill momentum continues building.
newsitem.headline: U.S. banking bill momentum continues building.

text.p: Banking legislation has a strong shot at passage before Congress adjourns as Republican leaders seek offsets for spending measures, Congressional aides and lobbyists said Monday.
The primary motivator is a realization that legislation to bolster the Savings Association Insurance Fund (SAIF) would offer budget-balancing funds to offset spending plans.
The legislation would require the thrift industry to pay a one-time charge totaling $4.7 billion to lift the SAIF to its mandated level.
That would amount to savings for Congressional budget balancing purposes of about $3 billion, a House aide said.
Chances were "enormously high" for passage, said Kenneth Guenther, of the Independent Bankers Association of America.

"The Republican leaders are inclined to give (President) Clinton the extra $6.3 billion for other programs that he wants," he said. "The trade-off for that is you have to find revenue offset and the (thrift fund) fix is a $3.1 billion revenue offset," Guenther said.
The banking legislation was expected to be added onto a broad spending bill to fund the government in fiscal 1997.
Interest payments on Financing Corp (FICO) bonds, issued in the late 1980s to help clean up failed thrifts, have been a draining force on the SAIF.
Legislation under consideration would require banks to share with thrifts the $793 million a year in interest payments on FICO bonds.

Bankers say that would cost their industry $10 billion to $12 billion over 20 years. They want provisions tacked on including regulatory relief and a clarification of lender liability laws for environmental clean-up costs of a business that defaults on its loan.
Bankers and insurance agents were duking it out over insurance provisions, with the agents trying to get them added onto the legislation and bankers working to keep them off.
Insurance agents said if regulatory relief measures are included in the legislation, they want provisions requiring bank employees selling insurance to be licensed by the state.

Bankers say the legislation has nothing to do with insurance interests. "The insurance stuff we regard as basically an outrage," Ed Yingling, executive vice president at the American Bankers Association, said.
The process was still fluid and final agreement between the House and Senate committees had yet to be inked.
Talks continued but no final agreement had yet been carved out, a House Banking Committee spokesman said. "Nothing has been agreed to on this side in final form," he said.
